title: Colossal squid chapter 3: The eyes and the hooks
sources: Te Papa, "Colossal squid" (tepapa.govt.nz/discover-collections/read-watch-play/science/colossal-squid-te-papa/): 2007 capture by San Aspiring, Ross Sea, toothfish at 1,500 m, tangled and dying, 495 kg weighed with ice, about 470 kg estimate, 1925 arm crowns in sperm whale stomach, beaks 38 mm (2003) and up to 49 mm, nine specimens above juvenile size since 1925, biology poorly known.
Mongabay 2008 (news.mongabay.com/2008/04/photos-researchers-study-largest-squid-ever-captured/) and RNZ 2018: 2007 specimen weight (494 kg / 470 kg), second source for the weight and capture.
Te Papa, anatomy and "Hooks and suckers" blog (blog.tepapa.govt.nz/2008/07/17/hooks-suckers/): tentacle hooks rotate 360 degrees, arm hooks do not, tentacles about 2 m.

Guinness World Records, "Largest eye" and Nilsson et al. 2012, Current Biology (adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012CBio...22..683N), plus Scientific American blog "Giant Eyes Help Colossal Squid Spot Glowing Whales": largest eyes of any living animal, about 27 to 28 cm on the 2007 specimen, spotting sperm whales from about 120 m.
Te Papa, shrinkage in the freezer for 14 months.

National Geographic, "First ever video shows colossal squid in natural habitat" (April 2025): 9 March 2025, Falkor (too), ROV SuBastian, about 1,968 ft (600 m), juvenile about a foot long, identified by hooks and chromatophores, adults up to about 7 m, 1925 first specimen from a sperm whale.

Yahoo/CNN, "Colossal squid resembles a glass sculpture" (April 2025) and NPR (15 April 2025): near South Sandwich Islands, about 30 cm, largely transparent, Bolstad and Evans verified, adults to 7 m and about 500 kg, most specimens from dead animals.

lines.text: Why would an animal need an eye that big?

lines.text: Down there, there is almost no light. A 2012 study in the journal Current Biology offered an idea.

lines.text: The researchers think that a big eye lets a squid spot a sperm whale coming, because the whale stirs up glowing sea life as it swims.
